newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast oil product outlook - under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Mideast oil product outlook - under pressure.

text.p: Premiums for second quarter Gulf middle distillates cargoes are vulnerable to further weakness because of limited sales opportunities to Asian markets, Gulf traders said Thursday.

Gas oil (diesel) and jet-kerosene premiums to independent price quotes fob Gulf for April and end March cargoes have fallen 5-10 cents in the week to below 50 cents a barrel, versus $1.00-$1.20 a year ago.
Pressure on premiums and prices had been prompted by India Oil Corp's (IOC) decision to buy just 570,000 tonnes of one-percent sulphur diesel in its first tender for April.
"The market had been hoping for anything around 800,000 tonnes...It came as a disappointment," one trader said.
The new Indian financial year had led to speculation that IOC would increase imports to replenish stock levels.

IOC has issued a new April tender for 270,000 tonnes of one-percent and 0.5-percent but these additional supplies would likely be sourced from the Mediterranean and Singapore when IOC awards the incremental tender on Wednesday, traders said.
East African and Gulf demand was flat and cargoes for end-March were still available and struggling to compete against Mediterranean supplies, they said.

News that Singapore refiners are enjoying their best returns in a year and that throughputs were to be increased to maximum to take advantage of high margins raised the prospect that Gulf products would find it more difficult to find Asian homes.
Gas oil was assessed at $23.50 fob Gulf on Thursday and jet-kerosene at $25.30, boosting margins for refiners in the region after crude's recent price fall.
Kerosene premiums were bid below 30 cents as heating demand fell off though the outlook for naphtha premiums remains bullish on the back of Far East petrochemical interest.
The seasonal downturn in heating demand was also reflected in Saudi Aramco's decision to cut its March propane price by $50 to $270 a tonne, its lowest level since November.

Naphtha's premium was talked at $13, compared to $6 last February while fuel oil held steady at a $5-6 discount despite further bunker price cuts by Saudi Aramco and a $3 drop in Fujairah 380-cst markets to $93 a tonne.
Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) has concluded term naphtha supplies between $13 and $13.50, Gulf traders said.
"It is above $13 but below $13.50," a source said.

The new term price with Japanese and Korean refiners, petrochemical firms and traders compares with the current premium of $6.50 for the one-year term that started a year ago and of $7.90 for August 1996-July 1997.
KPC, Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) are expected to resume term product talks in April.
